primary_outcome_name: AP RMS (anterior-posterior root mean square of center-of-pressure sway)
primary_outcome_instrument_scale: BTrackS force plate, COP-derived AP RMS in cm (continuous; log-transformed for analysis)
primary_timepoint: T4 (three months post-intervention); paper does not explicitly designate a single 'primary' timepoint, see notes
population_detail: Community-dwelling older adults aged >=60 years in the Greater Orlando, FL area, low-income status per 2019 US Census poverty thresholds, not receiving rehabilitation-facility treatment, able to stand unassisted; excluded if unable to perform physical activity, hospitalized more than 3 times in the last year, or did not speak English or Spanish. Not a clinically defined patient population; recruited as a general geriatric fall-risk-prevention sample (mean age 74.3 +/- 7.1 years, 88% female).

published_estimate.quote: Table 3. Results of linear mixed effects models fitted for all static balance metrics. AP RMS (Log-Transformed), Predictor 'Group * Time (T4)': Estimate 0.02, 95% CI (-0.08, 0.12), p = 0.678. (p. 8 of 16). Cf. also narrative text p. 8: 'AP RMS, ML RMS, and sway area did not significantly change across the four time points.'

B_covariate_list: Age, BMI, Sex, Race/ethnicity (plus random intercepts for Subject ID and Site; fixed effects for Timepoint (T1-T4, factor) and Group x Timepoint interaction)
data_availability_statement: Data Availability Statement: The deidentified data for this study, as well as the statistical processing code, is publicly available at https://osf.io/8763w/overview (created 25 October 2025).

registry_check.issues: AP_RMS is NOT the primary outcome of the underlying trial. The paper explicitly states: 'The primary outcomes of the trial itself were fall risk, dynamic balance, and physical activity levels, whereas the secondary outcomes were fall risk appraisal (comprising level of fear for falling and static balance performance) and negative self-perceptions of aging. In this exploratory analysis, the static balance of older adults was focused on...' This paper is explicitly labelled an 'exploratory analysis' of static balance (a sub-component of a secondary trial outcome), reporting four static balance metrics (AP RMS, ML RMS, sway speed variability, sway area) in parallel with no stated hierarchy/primary designation among them and no multiplicity correction across the resulting 4 outcomes x 3 time contrasts. AP RMS was chosen as 'the' outcome for our registry only because it is listed first in the Abstract's outcome list ('AP RMS, ML RMS, sway speed variability, and sway area') and in the Statistical Analysis section and Tables 3/4 order; however, the Introduction's closing paragraph lists the metrics in a different order ('sway area, AP root mean square (RMS), ML RMS, and COP sway speed variability'), i.e. sway area first -- so 'first-named outcome' is ambiguous depending on section. Notably, AP RMS shows no significant Group main effect (p=0.667) nor any significant Group*Time interaction at T2/T3/T4 (p=0.389/0.915/0.678); the paper's own emphasized findings are for sway area (marginal Group*Time(T2), Std beta=-0.07, p=0.050) and sway speed variability (significant Group*Time(T4), Std beta=0.10, p=0.014) -- i.e. not for AP RMS at all. Also, the observed statistical power for the AP RMS model is reported as only 22%, flagged by the authors themselves as a reason for caution. Primary_time=4 (T4) is not explicitly declared 'the' primary timepoint by the paper either; both short-term (T1-T2) and medium-term (T1-T4) effects are examined without hierarchy, though the registry's chosen contrast (Group*Time(T4) for AP RMS, raw/log-scale Estimate 0.02, p=0.678) matches Table 3 exactly, confirming which cell of the table the registry pulled from. Covariates (Age, BMI, Gender/Sex, Race) and cluster variable (Site) match the paper exactly (random effects for Subject ID and Site; fixed effects incl. age, BMI, sex, race/ethnicity). Control arm (educational CDC flyers, 'live their lives normally') matches. Time variable (T1-T4 long format) matches.

analysis_method_quote: 2.6. Statistical Analysis ... Anderson-darling tests found that the four static balance variables, as well as age and BMI, exhibited nonnormal distributions... A logarithmic transformation was applied to all balance variables to approximate a normal distribution for analysis. To account for the cluster-randomized design for this study, linear mixed effects models were fitted to the four continuous outcomes (AP RMS, ML RMS, sway speed variability, and sway area) to assess short- (T1-T2) and medium-term (T1-T4) effects through the 'lme' function in the 'lme4' package in RStudio [30]. Linear mixed effects models were chosen due to their robustness to violations in normality [31]. To account for any confounding effects, the following variables were considered as covariates for analysis: age, BMI, sex, and race/ethnicity. Each model consisted of random effects for the subject IDs assigned to each participant and the research sites that were included in this study, as well as fixed effects for group (intervention vs. control), timepoint (T1-T4), age, BMI, sex, race/ethnicity, and an interaction between group and timepoint. The models were optimized using the 'bobyqa' optimizer and utilized restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation to account for the random effects... Participants with missing data at various timepoints were included in the analysis, as linear mixed effects models can accommodate missing data [32,33]... Data are presented as mean +/- standard deviation unless indicated otherwise, and the threshold for significance was set at p < 0.05. (pp. 5-6 of 16, Section 2.6).
notes: This paper (Suarez et al., Geriatrics 2026, 11, 6; DOI 10.3390/geriatrics11010006) is an explicitly labelled EXPLORATORY secondary analysis of static balance outcomes from a cluster-randomized trial (NCT05778604, protocol: Thiamwong et al., JMIR Res Protoc 2023) whose registered PRIMARY outcomes are fall risk, dynamic balance, and physical activity levels -- none of which are reported in this paper. Static balance (of which AP RMS is one of four component metrics) was only a secondary outcome domain of the parent trial. Consequently there is no trial- or paper-declared 'primary' static balance metric; AP RMS was used for our registry/extraction purely by virtue of being listed first in the Abstract and Methods (Section 2.6) outcome lists and in Tables 3/4, while the Introduction lists sway area first instead -- flagged as an ambiguity per task instructions. n_randomised=404 is inferred from 'A total of 404 community-dwelling older adults across 17 different sites... were recruited for this study. Eligible participants were randomized by site into either the control or intervention group' (Section 2.3); the paper does not give a separate CONSORT-flow enrolled-vs-randomized breakdown in the extracted text (Figure 1 is a flow diagram image not captured by pdftotext). n_analysed_primary=373 is the analytic sample after excluding participants without static balance data at any of T1-T4 or with missing demographic data (matches Abstract: 'Among 373 community-dwelling older adults... mean age = 74.3 +/- 7.1 years'). Group-level n with available data varies by timepoint per Table 2 (Intervention T1 n=247, T4 n=193; Control T1 n=111, T4 n=83), distinct from the overall arm n reported in Table 1 (Intervention n=254, Control n=119) used in published_group_stats. Baseline imbalance was found for BMI and race/ethnicity (Table 1), but the covariate set (age, BMI, sex, race/ethnicity) was pre-specified in the Introduction before Results were presented, so this was coded as NOT a post-hoc adjustment triggered by the baseline test. Journal is 'Geriatrics' (MDPI, ISSN per DOI prefix 10.3390/geriatrics); MDPI mandates a Data Availability Statement section in all articles but it is unclear from the paper alone whether actual data/code deposit is journal-mandated versus author-voluntary, hence 'unclear' for journal_requires_data_sharing (a Data Availability Statement with a public OSF link is nonetheless present). No explicit ICH E9(R1)-style estimand language anywhere in the paper.
